title: A cloudy cluster in N11
caption: A young star cluster and dusty clouds in the Large Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: N11 · Large Magellanic Cloud · constellation Dorado · about 160,000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, C. Murray, J. Maíz Apellániz

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week, September 2025 (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Bright young stars light up clouds of gas and sculpt clumps of dust in this Hubble view of part of N11, the second-largest star-forming region in the Large Magellanic Cloud. That galaxy lies about 160,000 light-years away and is the largest of the dozens of small galaxies orbiting the Milky Way, with 10 to 20 percent of its mass.
The young stars’ powerful ultraviolet light shapes the clouds around them. In stellar nurseries like this one, gas clouds gather and collapse to form new stars.

The image combines observations made about 20 years apart. The first, from 2002 and 2003, used the then newly installed Advanced Camera for Surveys to catalog every star in this young cluster, from a tenth of the Sun’s mass to 100 times it, something not done before. The second, from Wide Field Camera 3, focused on the dusty clouds for a new look at cosmic dust.
scale: Using the source’s listed field of view (2.22 × 1.36 arcminutes) and its distance of about 160,000 light-years, the frame spans roughly 103 × 63 light-years. Its light set out about 160,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble’s cameras through three filters: blue, green and near-infrared. The color assigned to each filter isn’t published.
understand.eye: Ultraviolet and near-infrared light are invisible to the eye, and the colors are assigned, so the eye would not see this palette.

explore: The Large Magellanic Cloud’s biggest star factory is the Tarantula Nebula, a frequent Hubble target. Pairing data from two cameras two decades apart is possible because Hubble has been working for so long.
alt: A cluster of bright young stars among glowing clouds of gas and dark clumps of dust.
